title: DECEIVE-AFC: Adversarial Claim Attacks against Search-Enabled LLM-based Fact-Checking Systems
claim: Older systems match claims against a fixed evidence store with a static neural pipeline; newer ones use an LLM agent that dynamically plans, searches and synthesizes.
layout: 2 stacked panels split by dashed line, left-to-right flow, numbered modules in rounded box
description: The figure has two horizontal panels separated by a dashed line. The top panel, titled 'Traditional DNN-based AFC system', shows a left-to-right pipeline. A database labeled 'Pre-built Static Evidence Repository' and a claim document feed an Encoder trapezoid. The encoder outputs yellow evidence-representation vectors and blue claim-representation vectors. These pass through a Similarity block and stacked circle columns into neural-network icons, which produce a Verdict (check/cross) and a Justification clipboard. The bottom panel, titled 'Search-Enabled LLM-based AFC Systems', shows a claim feeding a robot-agent icon inside a large rounded box. Dashed bidirectional arrows link the agent to three colored modules: blue Search Plan/Query, orange Search Tool/Internet, and green Evidence Summarize/Search Results. These are numbered 1–3 and described in a left-hand legend. Outputs are Verdict and Justification on the right.
caption: Comparison between traditional DNN-based AFC systems and search-enabled LLM-based AFC systems.
abstract: Fact-checking systems with search-enabled large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for verifying claims by dynamically retrieving external evidence. However, the robustness of such systems against adversarial attack remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we study adversarial claim attacks against search-enabled LLM-based fact-checking systems under a realistic input-only threat model. We propose DECEIVE-AFC, an agent-based adversarial attack framework that integrates novel claim-level attack strategies and adversarial claim validity evaluation principles. DECEIVE-AFC systematically explores adversarial attack trajectories that disrupt search behavior, evidence retrieval, and LLM-based reasoning without relying on access to evidence sources or model internals. Extensive evaluations on benchmark datasets and real-world systems demonstrate that our attacks substantially degrade verification performance, reducing accuracy from 78.7% to 53.7%, and significantly outperform existing claim-based attack baselines with strong cross-system transferability.
